entries.title: 1. Input
entries.short: You receive new material — explanation, example or question from the AI.
entries.long:
## Step 1: Input

Every learning cycle starts with input. The AI presents
the material: an explanation, an example, an open
question or a situation — depending on the selected
method.

## What the AI does

- **In deductive**: explains the rule.
- **In inductive**: shows examples.
- **In error-based**: presents a problem with a trap.
- **In dialogic**: opens the conversation with a
  question.
- **In contextual**: sketches the scenario.

## What you do

Read attentively. Ask questions when something is
unclear — the session is a dialog, not a lecture. If you
find the AI's confidence too high, stay with it: some
explanations only land on the second read.

## What the dual-prompt evaluator does

It is running quietly. It observes your reaction (or
lack thereof) and assesses whether you absorbed the
material. Active scoring begins in step 2 (attempt).

## What happens if you race through this step

The most common beginner mistake: jumping to "action"
without processing the input. The system spots this from
low confidence on subsequent attempts — and sends you
back to step 1.

entries.title: 2. Attempt
entries.short: You apply what you learned to a concrete task or question.
entries.long:
## Step 2: Attempt

You get an application of the material and try to solve
it. First answer, first example, first concrete
application of the rule.

## What the AI does

The AI gives you a clearly scoped task. For language:
translate a sentence. For code: write a function. For
music: practice a chord change. Difficulty is
deliberately low — the first attempt should be
achievable.

## What you do

Try it. Even if you are unsure. An incomplete or
mistaken answer is more valuable than a refusal because
it gives the evaluator material to work with.

## Dual-prompt evaluator

It activates here. It reads your answer and assigns a
confidence score (0-100%). At high confidence you skip
straight to step 5 (adapt), bypassing error analysis. At
low confidence the path goes through step 3 (error) and
step 4 (feedback).

## Tip: do not stall

If you have no approach after 30 seconds, tell the AI
("I do not know where to start"). The AI gives you a
hint instead of the full solution — and the evaluator
does not count this as a failed attempt.

entries.title: 3. Error
entries.short: A mistake or misconception becomes visible.
entries.long:
## Step 3: Error

If your attempt in step 2 did not reach the target, the
cycle passes through this step. The error is named — not
judged, just marked as a learning opportunity.

## What the AI does

It shows you where the error is, without immediately
correcting it. The point: you should *see* the error,
not just *hear that something was wrong*. That
distinction determines whether you repeat the error.

## What you do

Trace the error. If you can correct it yourself, do so.
If not, signal that to the AI ("I do not understand
where the error is") — the next step (feedback) exists
to clarify.

## When no error appears

At high confidence in step 2, the cycle skips this step.
The system notes it and raises difficulty in the next
cycle — you should be challenged, not bored.

## In error-based (method)

If you chose this method, step 3 is the cycle's main
step. The AI deliberately leads you into typical traps
— see the methods glossary.

entries.title: 4. Feedback
entries.short: The AI explains why something works or does not work.
entries.long:
## Step 4: Feedback

Here comes the explanation. The AI describes the
principle behind your error or correct answer — ideally
so that you can transfer the principle to other cases.

## What good feedback contains

- **What happened** (description of the observation).
- **Why it happened** (explanation of the principle).
- **How to do it differently next time** (concrete
  action guidance).

Without (3), feedback evaporates. With (3), a correction
becomes a transferable rule.

## What you do

Read, follow, ask back. If feedback has not clicked yet,
say so. The AI is patient — it will explain the
principle in another variant. Better understood twice
than echoed once.

## Dual-prompt evaluator

It reads your reaction to the feedback. If you say "Ah,
now I understand" (or equivalent), confidence rises and
you proceed. If you still sound confused, the evaluator
pulls the cycle back to step 1 (input) with a new
explanation approach.

## Also on correct answers

Feedback is not only for errors. When you solved
something correctly, the AI still explains the
principle behind it — so the success becomes
transferable.

entries.title: 5. Adapt
entries.short: You adjust your strategy or understanding based on the feedback.
entries.long:
## Step 5: Adapt

You take what you learned from the feedback and adjust
your approach. Not just intellectually ("yes, now I
understand"), but operationally ("next time I will do it
differently").

## What happens here concretely

- **For language**: you rephrase. Instead of the wrong
  construction you use the corrected one.
- **For code**: you restructure the function with the
  understood principle.
- **For math**: you solve a variant using the corrected
  solution path.

## What the AI does

It gives you a *new* task — not the old one with the
known solution, but a variation that demands the
understood principle in a new context.

## Why this step matters

Understanding without adaptation evaporates. If you only
"echo" the feedback but do not build it into your
approach, you will repeat the error next time. Step 5
forces operational activation.

## Dual-prompt evaluator

Here it evaluates learning transfer. A successful
adaptation in a new variation is the best signal that
learning stuck — confidence typically rises above 80%.

entries.title: 6. Repeat
entries.short: You practice with variations until what you learned is fluent.
entries.long:
## Step 6: Repeat

You get more variations of the task. Not identical
repetition (that just leads to memorization), but
variation: same core, different context, different
difficulty.

## What the AI does

It generates tasks that test the same principle in
different guises. For language: different vocabulary,
different sentence structure, same grammar. For code:
different data, same algorithmic structure.

## Why variation, not repetition

Research on **interleaved practice** shows: blocked
practice (all tasks on the same topic in a row) creates
illusion of competence. Interleaved practice (related
tasks with variation) creates transferable knowledge.

## When the step ends

Once the dual-prompt evaluator sees three variations in
a row with confidence > 80%, you proceed to step 7. If
confidence fluctuates, the cycle stays in step 6 —
until stability is reached.

## Connection to spaced repetition

What you solve successfully in step 6 enters the
spaced-repetition system. The system schedules reviews
at 1 day, 3 days, 7 days, 14 days, 30 days — so the
learning sticks long-term.

entries.title: 7. Integrate
entries.short: You connect what you learned to other knowledge or a real application.
entries.long:
## Step 7: Integrate

The learning cycle ends with you placing the new
learning into a larger context. Not in isolation
("today I learned this") but connected to what you
already knew.

## What the AI does

It challenges you to link the new content to other
concepts or apply it in a real scenario:

- **Language**: use the tense in a free conversation.
- **Code**: apply the new technique in a larger project.
- **Theory**: combine the concept with one of your own
  questions.

## What you do

Articulate the required link. Find your own examples.
Reach the point where you can say: "I can do this now —
not because I memorized it, but because I can deploy
it."

## What happens after step 7

The cycle is complete. Three options:

- **End the session** and rate it (understanding /
  stress / method fit).
- **Auto-loop**: a new cycle with a new topic starts
  automatically.
- **Method switch**: at low method fit the system
  recommends a method change for the next cycle.

## Why the system closes here

Integration is the only robust test that learning
worked. Memorized content fails in step 7; understood
knowledge thrives here.
